planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants after all danger of frost in dappled or morning sun with afternoon shade; this compact Swedish-bred selection stays low and full without pinching, making it well suited to pots and border edges rather than mass beds.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from harsh midday sun. Mona Wallhed is a dwarf, tightly mounding crossandra selection bred for pot culture that stays under 18 inches, distinguishing it from the taller, looser habit of the species and from the coral-orange tones of Orange Marmalade by producing closely packed spikes of soft salmon-pink, fan-shaped flowers over neat, glossy foliage. Its dense branching habit needs little pinching to stay full, and it blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall in warm, humid conditions. Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist, since crossandra sulks and drops buds if allowed to dry out repeatedly.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Yellow Queen has a lower, more sprawling habit than the red-bracted species and works well as a groundcover or spilling over a container edge.

directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil. Yellow Queen is a low, sprawling shrimp plant selection that replaces the species' salmon-red bracts with long-lasting chartreuse-to-butter-yellow bracts, from which small white two-lipped true flowers emerge continuously from spring through fall. Its shorter, spreading habit sets it apart from the more upright red and white shrimp plant forms already common in the trade, making it useful as a mounding groundcover or edging plant rather than a background shrub. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit readily; prune lightly after bloom flushes to keep the mound tidy.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container specimens in spring in moist, well-drained soil in dappled sun to partial shade; Fruit Cocktail is noted for tolerating brief hard freezes better than typical shrimp plant cultivars, resprouting reliably from the roots in zone 9.

directions: Plant in dappled sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil. Fruit Cocktail is a multicolor shrimp plant selection whose overlapping bracts open golden-lime green and age through soft yellow and blush tones, with pink-to-red two-lipped true flowers emerging from the bract tips — a candy-colored departure from the solid salmon-red or plain yellow bracts of other shrimp plant forms. The mixed-color bract effect is most pronounced when spikes are examined at different ages on the same plant, since new and older bracts persist together. It attracts hummingbirds and butterflies and benefits from an annual hard pruning in late winter to renew flowering wood.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; the variegated leaves scorch and lose their white margins faster than plain-green shrimp plant cultivars if exposed to hot, direct afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil. Unlike other shrimp plant selections grown primarily for bract color, Variegata is grown chiefly for its foliage — leaves emerge pale chartreuse-green in spring and mature to green broadly edged and splashed in creamy white, giving the plant garden interest even between bloom flushes. Salmon-orange, shrimp-shaped bract spikes appear against the pale foliage from spring through fall, with white tubular true flowers peeking from the bract tips. The clump-forming habit and lighter coloring make it a good choice for brightening shaded containers, hanging baskets, and mixed borders where a plain green backdrop would look heavy. Cut back stems that revert to solid green to keep the variegation strong.
sources: San Marcos Growers nursery reference database

planting.note: Set out after the last frost in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; this yellow-flowered dwarf grows and blooms at the same slow, compact pace as the better-known Dwarf Red form of the species.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun and keep evenly moist while roots establish. Dwarf Yellow is the yellow-flowered counterpart to Ixora taiwanensis 'Dwarf Red', sharing the same tight, boxwood-leaved, slow-growing mound but replacing the red blooms with rounded, 3–5-inch clusters of soft, buttery-yellow florets from late spring into fall. The yellow coloring reads as softer and more pastel than the golden-orange tones of Ixora 'Maui', making it a distinct color option among compact ixoras for edging and low massing. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer and watch for interveinal chlorosis in alkaline Gulf Coast soils, treating with chelated iron as needed.
